subject: Climate & Environment
title: Small Wind and Community Power
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Small Wind and Community Power.

hook.text: Not all wind turbines are giants. Some are small enough to fit on a rooftop.

buildup.text: Small turbines power farms, schools, and remote villages that the grid cannot reach.

discovery.text: Community wind projects let neighbors co-own a turbine and split the electricity.

twist.text: Denmark gets 50% of its power from wind — much of it from community-owned projects.

climax.text: Local ownership means profits stay in the town instead of going to distant utilities.

punchline.text: When the town owns the turbine, everyone shares the wind.

quiz.question: What percentage of Denmark's power comes from wind?

details.summary: Small wind turbines and community-owned wind projects bring renewable energy to rural areas and small towns. Community ownership models allow local residents to invest in and benefit from wind projects, distributing economic gains more broadly than large corporate installations.
details.whyItMatters: Community energy empowers local populations and builds public support for renewables. Shared ownership models demonstrate that the energy transition can be inclusive and equitable.
takeaways: Small turbines suit farms, schools, and remote communities
Community ownership distributes financial benefits locally
Local projects build public acceptance of wind energy

faq.question: How do community wind projects work?
faq.answer: Residents pool funds or form cooperatives to finance turbines on shared or leased land. Electricity is sold to the grid, and profits are returned as dividends or reinvested locally. Denmark pioneered this model and it is now widespread in Germany and Scotland.

faq.question: Are small wind turbines economical?
faq.answer: Small turbines cost more per kilowatt than large ones, but they can be cost-effective in windy locations with high electricity prices and limited grid access. Government incentives and net metering policies improve their financial viability.
